message.content:
**The three most widely‑recognized “great” schisms in Christian history are:** | # | Schism | Approximate dates | Key causes & consequences | |---|--------|-------------------|---------------------------| | **1** | **The Great Schism (East–West Schism)** | 1054 CE | • Long‑standing theological, liturgical, and political differences between the Byzantine (Eastern) and Latin (Western) churches.
• Disputes over the *Filioque* clause, papal primacy, and ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
• Resulted in the formal split of the Christian world into the Roman Catholic Church (West) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (East). | | **2** | **The Protestant Reformation** | 1517 – 1648 CE | • Initiated by Martin Luther’s 95 Theses (1517) and spread through the Reformation in Germany, Switzerland, England, France, and beyond.
• Criticized papal authority, indulgences, and other practices; emphasized *sola fide* (faith alone) and *sola scriptura* (scripture alone).
• Produced a wide array of Protestant denominations (Lutheran, Calvinist/Reformed, Anglican, Anabaptist, etc.) and led to the Counter‑Reformation within Catholicism. | | **3** | **The Old Catholic Schism** | 1870 – present | • Sparked by the First Vatican Council’s declaration of papal infallibility (1870).
• A group of bishops and clergy in several European countries rejected the doctrine and formed the *Old Catholic Church* (e.g., the Union of Utrecht).
• While smaller in size than the previous two schisms, it remains a significant break from Rome and has maintained its own distinct traditions and ecumenical relations. | These three events are often cited as the “great” schisms because each fundamentally reshaped the structure, theology, and global distribution of Christianity.
